notes: All 15 assertions passed in both configurations across all 3 cases (30/30) — none of the current assertions discriminate with_skill from without_skill on this codebase. The existing repo already wires the conventions the assertions check (role claim in the JWT, DTO pattern, service-layer delegation), so a capable baseline model follows them without the skill's explicit instructions. This isn't a sign the skill is useless — it's a sign these 3 evals, on this particular well-structured codebase, don't yet create a situation where only the skill's guidance prevents a wrong answer. A future iteration should either test on a messier/less-idiomatic codebase, or add assertions that check for things the skill uniquely prescribes (e.g. the exact 8-phase explain-before/report-after structure, or a specific security requirement baseline Claude might skip, like PKCE/state validation commentary) rather than outcomes a competent engineer reaches either way.

with_skill used more tokens on every one of the 3 cases (mean 99,085 vs 92,577, +7%) and was NOT reliably faster — it was slower on the refresh-token case specifically (894s vs 775s) despite landing on a comparable implementation. This is consistent with the skill's explicit phase-by-phase narration (8 workflow phases, explain-before/summarize-after on each) adding verbosity without a corresponding quality payoff visible in these assertions.

Qualitative difference not captured by any assertion: the with_skill refresh-token run added a GlobalExceptionHandler (@RestControllerAdvice) to centralize the new error's JSON shape, consistent with the existing RestAuthenticationEntryPoint/RestAccessDeniedHandler pattern; the without_skill run handled the error inline in the controller instead. Minor, but a real architectural-consistency edge for with_skill worth preserving if assertions are tightened.

Grading in this iteration is based on each subagent's self-reported final text (SubagentHandback), not an independently read transcript or file diff — every subagent's Write tool refused its REPORT.md path with 'Subagents should return findings as text, not write report files,' so the orchestrator persisted the hand-backed text itself. This is a tooling constraint on this run, not an evidence-quality endorsement: a stronger grading pass would diff the actual changed files in each isolated project copy under spring-oauth2-backend-repos/ rather than trust the executor's account of what it did.

The RBAC case's 5th assertion ('explained before implementing... reported real outcome') is weakly discriminating for the same reason: without a transcript, grading can't tell an agent that explained before coding from one that reconstructed a plausible-sounding explanation into its final report afterward. Both RBAC runs passed it, but the with_skill run's report was structured as explicit numbered phases while the without_skill run's was narrative — if this distinction matters, the assertion should require transcript evidence specifically.
